title: Two Sum: return indices of pair summing to target (HashMap of complement).
shortTitle: Two Sum: Return Indices of a Pair Summing to Target
keyPoints: For each element, compute the complement (target minus value) and check a HashMap of already-seen values; a hit gives the answer pair.
Check for the complement before inserting the current value to avoid pairing an element with itself.
Average O(n) time and O(n) space because each HashMap lookup and insert is O(1) average.
The brute-force double loop is O(n squared) and only acceptable for tiny inputs.
For sorted input, a two-pointer approach uses O(1) extra space but loses original indices.
For BigDecimal keys, normalise scale before insertion so that numerically equal complements are found.

s1_definition.oneliner: For each value, look up target minus value in a HashMap of seen values; a hit is the answer, otherwise record the value and move on.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Two Sum** – find the indices of two elements in an array that add up to a given target.
- **Complement** – for a current value `v`, the complement is `target - v`, the value needed to complete the pair.
- **HashMap approach** – scan once, storing each value and its index; for each element check if its complement is already in the map.
- **Time complexity** – O(n) average because each map lookup and insert is O(1) average.
- **Space complexity** – O(n) for the map, trading memory for speed over the O(n squared) brute force.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to find two transactions on Rajesh's account that together make up a suspicious round figure flagged by the fraud rules. Instead of comparing every transaction against every other, a clerk walks the list once holding a notebook of amounts already seen and where they were. For each new transaction the clerk works out how much would be needed to reach the target and checks the notebook. If that complement is already noted, the pair is found. One pass, with a quick notebook lookup each time.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Two Sum asks for the indices of two elements that add up to a target, and the efficient solution is a single pass with a HashMap from value to index. For each element I compute the complement, which is the target minus the current value, and I check whether that complement is already in the map. If it is, the stored index and the current index are the answer. Otherwise I record the current value and index and move on. It is average O(n) time, which beats the O(n squared) brute-force double loop.

The ordering detail that keeps it correct is that I check for the complement before inserting the current value. That way an element is never paired with itself. If the same value legitimately appears twice and the target is twice that value, the second occurrence finds the first because it was stored on the previous iteration.

I note the alternative: on sorted data, a two-pointer approach uses O(1) extra space, but it needs sorting which costs O(n log n) or loses the original indices. When the problem wants original indices on unsorted data, the HashMap approach is the right default. For money I use BigDecimal keys and normalise scale, because BigDecimal equals considers scale and would otherwise miss a numerically equal complement.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India, I used this in the fraud engine to detect a split-into-two evasion pattern: finding whether any two transactions on Rajesh's account add up exactly to a flagged target and reporting which two. Amounts are BigDecimal with possible scale differences, so I normalise the keys.

Remember one sentence: store each value's index in a HashMap and look up the complement (target minus current) before inserting, giving O(n) pair detection in one pass.
